hints: Focus on what happens when Period 3 chlorides meet water, do they ever make alkaline solutions?
Recall that $\text{NaCl}$ gives pH 7, $\text{MgCl}_2$ gives weakly acidic pH around 6, and $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{SiCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ all give strongly acidic solutions.
Compare that pH trend with the high melting points of ionic chlorides, then ask if any single chloride can be both pH 12 and melt as described.
walkthrough:
**List the possible Period 3 chlorides**

Think of the family from left to right across Period 3. You have ionic $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{MgCl}_2$, then $\text{AlCl}_3$, then covalent $\text{SiCl}_4$, $\text{PCl}_3$, $\text{PCl}_5$ and chlorides of sulfur.

No Period 3 chloride contains a strong base, so keep that in mind.

**Check the pH on dissolving in water**

This is the key test. Chlorides hydrolyse to give neutral or acidic solutions only.

$$\text{NaCl(aq)} \rightarrow \text{pH} \approx 7 \text{ (neutral)}$$ $$\text{MgCl}_2\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{pH} \approx 6 \text{ (weak hydrolysis of Mg}^{2+})$$ $$\text{AlCl}_3, \text{SiCl}_4, \text{PCl}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl(aq)} \text{, pH 1 to 3 (strongly acidic)}$$

**Check appearance and melting**

A white crystalline solid with a high melting point fits an ionic chloride like $\text{NaCl}$ (mp $801^{\circ}\text{C}$) or $\text{MgCl}_2$ (mp $714^{\circ}\text{C}$). These could soften or melt after prolonged strong heating in a test-tube.

Covalent chlorides like $\text{SiCl}_4$ is a liquid and $\text{PCl}_5$ sublimes and fumes, so they do not fit as well.

**Spot the contradiction**

No Period 3 chloride can give pH 12. A pH 12 means strongly alkaline, which would need free $\text{OH}^-$ ions, but dissolving a chloride can only give $\text{Cl}^-$ and acidic cations plus $\text{HCl}$.

So the white solid and melting parts might fit $\text{NaCl}$ or $\text{MgCl}_2$, but the pH 12 cannot be right. At least one observation must be incorrect.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. No Period 3 chloride gives an alkaline solution, let alone pH 12. Since the other details could fit an ionic chloride, the pH record (or another detail) must be wrong.
options.B: $\text{MgCl}_2$ is a white crystalline solid with a high melting point, but its solution is slightly acidic (pH about 5 to 6) due to hydrolysis of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, not pH 12. Students choosing this may focus only on appearance and melting and forget the pH trend.
options.C: $\text{PCl}_5$ is a pale solid that hydrolyses violently to give phosphoric acid and $\text{HCl}$, so pH 1 to 2, strongly acidic. It also sublimes rather than melting cleanly on heating. It is the opposite of pH 12.
options.D: $\text{NaCl}$ is a white crystalline solid with high melting point and dissolves easily, but it gives a neutral solution of pH 7. It never gives pH 12 because $\text{Na}^+$ does not hydrolyse to produce $\text{OH}^-$. Students choosing this may remember the appearance but miss the pH rule.
